transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-21
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~40 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Gomez (BlueHarbor Head of ML), Jamal Price (Platform Eng), Sofia Rivera (Sr. ML Eng)

--- Auto-generated Summary (optional) ---
Focus: TTFT and tail latency, streaming vs chunked responses, seq-len impacts, kernel selection and quantization tradeoffs.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh let's do a quick roll call. Maya here from Redwood, ravi with me from the SE team.
[00:08] Elena Gomez: hi, elena here.
[00:09] Jamal Price: jamal on platform.
[00:10] Sofia Rivera: sofia, ml eng.
[00:12] Maya Chen: awesome, quick agenda: review last week's perf runs, talk TTFT and streaming behavior, discuss kernel choices for the models you're testing, and agree next steps.

[02:15] Ravi Patel: okay so i pulled the runs you shared — thanks for the logs — ran them with streaming enabled and also with streaming disabled to compare TTFT. rough numbers: median TTFT for streaming + small-chunking was ~120-160ms on our test harness for the v1 model at 512 token context, 95th around 420ms. non-streaming cold TTFTs jump to ~320-380ms. so streaming gives you a decent time-to-first-token improvement but you need to watch chunk size.

[03:05] Sofia Rivera: when you say chunk size, do you mean the partial-token chunking or the application-level chunk? we've got our frontend reassembling partials so we can do smaller chunks.

[03:20] Ravi Patel: yeah both — there's the runtime chunk (how many tokens per stream write) and then the network chunking. if you stream too small, overhead per write increases and increases overall tail. we found 32 token chunks hit a good sweet spot in our infra for these models.

[05:00] Jamal Price: quick question — TTFT numbers you quoted, are those cold-starts or steady-state? our main problem is tail latency during bursts.

[05:17] Ravi Patel: good call — those medians are steady-state after JVM warm caches etc. cold-starts on fresh containers or after model load can be much higher — 900ms to multiple seconds depending on model size and quantization. for your POC cluster we recommend pre-warmed pods or reserved capacity.

[06:10] Elena Gomez: right, we were testing on a small pool of pre-warmed nodes but had autoscale kick in during a spike and saw user-facing spikes. is that where dedicated helps?

[06:30] Maya Chen: yes dedicated capacity avoids model load jitter as long as you keep some headroom. also we can configure keeps-alives and faster model-resident packing so K/V caches persist.

[07:05] Ravi Patel: another big lever is kernel selection. for the 7B family you're using, we recommend the fp16 vectorized kernels on A100 for best latency; if you want cost savings the int8 QAT path is promising but the TTFT can regress a bit unless you adjust the kernel tiling.

[07:40] Sofia Rivera: we're using the open-7b-quantized profile we got from last week's tests — which kernel would you pick for that?

[07:52] Ravi Patel: for that specific quant profile use the optimized int8 kernel with layer norm fusion enabled, and enable the per-layer fallback for attention on long sequence lengths. that keeps TTFT low for short prompts and avoids tail blowups on 2k+ sequences.

[09:10] Elena Gomez: sequence length — we pushed some logs. our 95th percentile seq length is about 420 tokens but there are tails up to 2,500 tokens during refunds flows. how do we guard the system?

[09:28] Ravi Patel: two main options: route long sequences to a higher-capacity pool or truncate/prefix to a summarization step. we also have kernel variants that trade per-token throughput for lower per-request latency for long sequences. you can also enable KV cache sticky routing so continuation requests hit the same worker.

[11:00] Jamal Price: sticky routing — is that compatible with autoscaling? what about deployment topology?

[11:14] Maya Chen: yes sticky routing is compatible but you need a small standing pool to keep cache locality; autoscaler can scale non-sticky workers independently. we can show config examples in the ops docs.

[12:45] Ravi Patel: another observation: your test harness shows batching set to pretty aggressive values (batch max 64). for latency-sensitive endpoints we usually do lower batch sizes (8-16) and enable dynamic batching with max_wait ~10ms. that helps TTFT and reduces tail jitter.

[13:30] Sofia Rivera: hmm we thought bigger batches reduced cost, but it hurt our 99th. seems like a tradeoff.

[13:40] Ravi Patel: exactly — cost vs latency. Redwood Optimize can give recommendations per-route based on your observed seq-len distribution. i'll add those numbers to the spreadsheet.

[15:02] Elena Gomez: can you remind us on quantization impact on accuracy? we've seen a small drop in some intent classification tests.

[15:18] Ravi Patel: yeah int8 can introduce minor regressions; we recommend running a small eval set against the quantized variant. sometimes int8 with per-channel scaling and some layers left in fp16 keeps quality within acceptable delta. SE will produce a recommended quant profile per model.

[16:00] Jamal Price: logs — what do you need from our side to reproduce the higher tails? we can share traces but there might be PII.

[16:12] Maya Chen: send sanitized request/response traces and the perf harness logs. if you can't sanitize, we can set up a secure upload or use a private S3 with KMS. also the CSV with seq-length distribution and request timestamps is super helpful.

[18:00] Ravi Patel: one more thing — streaming behavior in browsers: the client often waits to render until a chunk boundary or newline. consider emitting earlier tokens that let the UI render skeleton; that reduces perceived TTFT.

[18:35] Sofia Rivera: our frontend dev said they can render partials, we'll coordinate on chunk sizes.

[20:00] Ravi Patel: performance baseline i've put into the spreadsheet: model v1 (7B quant) streaming 32-token chunks median TTFT 140ms, p95 420ms, p99 750ms. non-streaming cold median 350ms. note these are on A100 reserved pool with fp16 kernels. i'll upload the raw numbers.

[21:30] Elena Gomez: can you also include a column for network RTT assumptions? our infra sits in eu-west and rtt adds ~50ms.

[21:45] Ravi Patel: yes will add region-specific adjustments.

[23:00] Maya Chen: security question — you'll need SOC2 and SSO. we've already sent core security docs, but i can link the SOC2 and ISO papers again and a contact for our security engineering.

[23:20] Elena Gomez: please, and add details about KMS integration for key management.

[23:30] Maya Chen: noted — i'll include KMS/HSM notes and the dedicated deployment checklist.

[25:00] Jamal Price: about dedicated trial — can we get a small dedicated pool for the week of the 4th to run full-scale tests?

[25:12] Maya Chen: yes we can provision a short dedicated trial; i'll send pricing and the exact capacity options in the follow-up.

[27:10] Ravi Patel: operationally, if you want ultra-low TTFT, we recommend: pre-warmed pods, 32-token streaming chunks, fp16 kernels for critical flows, sticky KV cache for session continuation, and smaller batching for latency-critical routes.

[28:00] Sofia Rivera: sounds good. for the 2.5k token tail we'll probably route those to a separate route with high-throughput kernels.

[29:15] Maya Chen: ok recap — ravi will share spreadsheet + kernel recommendations; sofia runs the 1k streaming TTFT test and uploads logs; maya to send pricing and security docs. follow-up scheduled next week same time unless we need earlier.

[30:10] Elena Gomez: quick flag — our product team wants a simple SLA note on allowed 95th latency for the pilot. can you draft a one-page note?

[30:22] Maya Chen: yes we'll draft an SLA note showing target medians and 95th guidance for the trial. not a legal SLA but a pilot target.

[31:00] Jamal Price: one more — any recommended kernel for the refund flow (long sequences)?

[31:10] Ravi Patel: for long sequences use the high-throughput kernel with attention chunking; it increases time per token slightly but keeps tail stable. i'll list exact kernel IDs in the sheet.

[33:00] Sofia Rivera: logistics — i'll need a sample curl / streaming client example to integrate; do you have SDK snippets?

[33:12] Maya Chen: yes code snippets and streaming examples are in the docs; i'll attach a quickstart repo link in the follow-up.

[35:00] (brief cross-talk about next week scheduling)

[36:00] Ravi Patel: final note — if you decide to go int8 for cost we should run a quality eval first; if accuracy delta > 1.5% we'll recommend partial fp16 layers.

[37:20] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. any other questions?

[37:25] Elena Gomez: none here, thanks.

[37:30] Jamal Price: all good.

[37:33] Sofia Rivera: thanks y'all.

[37:40] Maya Chen: great, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and docs, and catch up next week. bye.

--- End of transcript ---
